verses.text: When we were safe on land, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The people who lived there were very kind to us. It was raining and cold, so they built a fire and welcomed us all.
Paul gathered a pile of sticks and was putting them on the fire. A poisonous snake came out because of the heat and bit him on the hand.
The people of the island saw the snake hanging from Paul's hand. They said to each other, "This man must be a murderer! He escaped from the sea, but Justice will not let him live."
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and was not hurt at all.
The people waited for him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after waiting a long time, they saw that nothing bad happened to him. So they changed their minds and said he was a god.
Near that place there were fields that belonged to Publius, the most important man on the island. He welcomed us into his home and was very kind to us for three days.
Publius's father was in bed, sick with fever and a bad stomach illness. Paul went in to see him. He prayed, put his hands on him and healed him.
After this happened, all the other sick people on the island came to Paul, and they were healed too.
They gave us many gifts to honour us. When we were ready to sail, they put on the ship everything we needed.
After three months we set sail on a ship from Alexandria that had stayed at the island for the winter. The ship had the sign of the twin gods on its front.
We landed at Syracuse and stayed there three days.
From there we sailed around and came to Rhegium. The next day a south wind began to blow, and the day after that we reached Puteoli.
There we found some believers, and they asked us to stay with them for seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The believers in Rome heard that we were coming, and they came out to meet us as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Inns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and felt encouraged.
When we arrived in Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

Three days later Paul called together the Jewish leaders in Rome. When they had gathered, he said to them, "Brothers, I have done nothing against our people or against the customs of our ancestors. But I was arrested in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.
The Romans questioned me and wanted to set me free, because I had done nothing that deserved death.
But the Jews were against it, so I had to appeal to Caesar. I do not have any charge to bring against my own people.
That is why I asked to see you and talk with you. I am wearing this chain because of the hope of Israel."
They answered him, "We have not received any letters about you from Judea. And none of the brothers who came from there has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we want to hear what you think. We know that people everywhere are speaking against this group."

They agreed on a day to meet with Paul, and even more of them came to the house where he was staying. From morning until evening he explained God's Kingdom to them. He tried to convince them about Jesus from the law of Moses and from the Prophets.
Some of them believed what he said, but others did not.
They could not agree with each other, and they began to leave. Then Paul said one more thing: "The Holy Spirit was right when he spoke to your ancestors through Isaiah the prophet.
He said, 'Go to these people and say: You will listen and listen, but never understand. You will look and look, but never see.

These people's hearts have become hard. Their ears can hardly hear, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn to me, and I would heal them.'
So I want you to know that God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!"
When he had said this, the Jews left, arguing strongly among themselves.
For two whole years Paul stayed there in a house he rented. He welcomed everyone who came to see him.
He boldly preached God's Kingdom and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ, and no one tried to stop him.
